Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Brown sugar: White sugar with molasses added back, giving it moisture and a caramel taste, which is why cookies made with it come out chewier.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Caster sugar: A British fine-grained sugar that dissolves fast and so is preferred for meringues and sponges; the name comes from sugar casters, shakers.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Icing sugar: Also known as powdered or confectioners' sugar, it is ground very fine and usually mixed with a bit of cornstarch to prevent clumping.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Demerara: A pale golden raw cane sugar with large crystals, named for the Demerara region of Guyana, where it was first produced.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Muscovado: An unrefined cane sugar that is dark, sticky and rich in molasses, with a strong toffee flavor, widely used in gingerbread.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Turbinado: A light-brown raw sugar made by spinning cane juice crystals in a turbine, and is partly refined, with the name from the machine.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Granulated sugar: The standard white table sugar, refined to about 99.9 percent sucrose, and sucrose is made of glucose and fructose bonded.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Palm sugar: Made from boiled palm tree sap, it is a staple of Thai and Indonesian cooking, and sold in hard cakes or soft pastes.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Jaggery: An unrefined cane or palm sugar from South Asia, sold in blocks, and in India it is eaten after meals and offered at festivals.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Rock sugar: Large clear crystals grown on strings for days, used in Chinese cooking and teas, and said to give a gentler sweetness.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Coconut sugar: Made from the sap of coconut palm flowers, it is sold as a health option, but it has nearly the same calories as ordinary sugar.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Stevia: A trap: a sweetener from leaves of a South American plant, up to about 300 times sweeter than sugar, and it is not a sugar.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Aspartame: An artificial sweetener, about 200 times sweeter than sugar, discovered in 1965 by a chemist testing an ulcer drug, so it is not a type of sugar.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Sucralose: Made by chemically altering sugar, it is about 600 times sweeter and passes through the body mostly unabsorbed, so it counts as a sweetener.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Saccharin: The first artificial sweetener, found by accident in 1879 at Johns Hopkins when a chemist noticed a sweet taste on his hands.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Xylitol: A sugar alcohol used in gum, it is toxic to dogs, and counts as a sweetener rather than a sugar.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Monk fruit: A small melon from southern China, whose extract is hundreds of times sweeter than sugar, and a sweetener.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Cornstarch: A thickener from corn, not sweet at all; it is a white powder that thickens sauces when heated in liquid.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Baking soda: Sodium bicarbonate is a leavening agent, which reacts with acids to make bubbles, and has no sugar in it.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Salt: Salt is not sweet and has no relation to sugar, though a pinch of it enhances sweetness in baking.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).MSG: Monosodium glutamate adds savory umami flavor, discovered by Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda in 1908 and is not a sugar.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Erythritol: A sugar alcohol found naturally in some fruits, about 70 percent as sweet as sugar and almost calorie-free, so a sweetener.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Citric acid: The sour compound in lemons and limes, which adds tang and acts as a preservative, not a sweet one.
Types of sugar (not sweeteners).Cream of tartar: A powdery acid left over from winemaking, it stabilizes whipped egg whites, and has no sweetness.

Words for a female animal.Doe: A female deer. The word also covers rabbits and goats, and a doe usually gives birth to one or two fawns, sometimes three.
Words for a female animal.Ewe: A female sheep. The word comes from Old English and is pronounced like you, a sound shared with the pronoun.
Words for a female animal.Mare: A grown female horse. A pregnant mare carries her foal for about 11 months.
Words for a female animal.Sow: A female pig, which can have up to about 12 to 16 piglets in a litter. The word is pronounced like cow.
Words for a female animal.Hen: A female chicken, but also the word for the female of many birds. A hen can lay about 250 to 300 eggs a year.
Words for a female animal.Vixen: A female fox. A vixen is mostly known for her haunting screams in winter, used to call mates.
Words for a female animal.Jenny: A female donkey. Crossing a jenny with a male horse creates a hinny, while a mare and a jack produce a mule.
Words for a female animal.Nanny: A female goat. The nanny goat gave her name to the childcare worker, from the 18th century slang.
Words for a female animal.Cow: A female cattle or other large animals, such as elephants and whales. Cows form close friendships with certain herd mates.
Words for a female animal.Filly: A young female horse, typically under four years. The word is also old slang for a lively girl.
Words for a female animal.Lioness: A female lion. Lionesses do most of the hunting for the pride, often working as a group.
Words for a female animal.Tigress: A female tiger, a solitary hunter. A tigress raises cubs alone and teaches them to hunt.
Words for a female animal.Drake: A male duck. In breeding season he often has bright green head feathers, while the female stays mostly brown.
Words for a female animal.Buck: A male deer, goat, rabbit or kangaroo. Only the male deer grow antlers, shedding them every winter.
Words for a female animal.Ram: A male sheep. The ram's curled horns keep growing throughout its life, and stay on.
Words for a female animal.Stallion: A male horse. A wild stallion guards a harem of mares and fights rivals for them.
Words for a female animal.Boar: A male pig, or the wild ancestor of the domestic pig. Boars have tusks that grow throughout their lives.
Words for a female animal.Gander: A male goose. Ganders can fiercely guard the nest, and geese often mate for life.
Words for a female animal.Bull: A male cow, elephant, whale, or similar. A bull is a trap here, since it's male, not female.
Words for a female animal.Cob: A male swan, who helps defend the nest. The female swan is called a pen.
Words for a female animal.Tom: A male cat, but also a male turkey. A tom turkey fans his tail and gobbles to attract hens, while a hen only clucks.
Words for a female animal.Rooster: A male chicken, famous for crowing at dawn. The female is the hen.
Words for a female animal.Colt: A young male horse, usually under four years old. A young female is a filly, so this one is male and not a match.
Words for a female animal.Fawn: A baby deer, of either sex. It's not specifically female, so it does not belong on this list.

Noises a cat makes.Meow: Adult cats mostly meow to humans rather than each other. Kittens meow to their mothers, and some cats vary tone by demand.
Noises a cat makes.Purr: Cats purr when content but also when stressed or hurt. The frequency of the purr, 25 to 150 Hz, may help bones heal.
Noises a cat makes.Hiss: A warning that mimics a snake's sound. Cats hiss to say back off when scared or cornered.
Noises a cat makes.Yowl: A long, loud, drawn-out cry, often from cats in heat or those that are distressed, or from older cats that are confused.
Noises a cat makes.Trill: A short, rising, bubbly sound, used by mother cats to call kittens and by friendly cats to greet people.
Noises a cat makes.Growl: A low rumble that warns another animal to keep away. Cats growl when angry, scared or protecting food.
Noises a cat makes.Mew: A soft, high meow, especially kittens' call to their mother. The word is a bit old-fashioned.
Noises a cat makes.Caterwaul: A shrill, wailing cry, as of cats fighting at night. The word has been in English for centuries and also means to quarrel noisily.
Noises a cat makes.Spit: A sharp burst of air, used with a hiss as a defensive warning. It is a startled threat and means a cat is scared.
Noises a cat makes.Chirp: A short sound cats make when they watch birds, which scientists think expresses excitement and frustration.
Noises a cat makes.Moo: A cow's sound, not a cat's. Some cats that talk a lot might imitate it, but it is not a typical noise.
Noises a cat makes.Neigh: A horse's call. It carries long distances, and horses can recognise each other's neigh.
Noises a cat makes.Oink: A pig's sound, and a symbol for pigs in comic strips. Pigs actually make many other grunts and squeals.
Noises a cat makes.Quack: A duck's sound. Only female mallards make the classic loud quack, while males make quieter, raspier sounds.
Noises a cat makes.Baa: A sheep's cry, and not a cat's. Lambs call their mothers this way and are recognised by their own mother's voice.
Noises a cat makes.Woof: A dog's bark. It is a trap since cats do not woof, though some very big cats may produce a huff.
Noises a cat makes.Bark: A dog sound, and the cat's cousins rarely make it. Dogs bark far more than their wolf ancestors, probably a result of domestication.
Noises a cat makes.Croak: A frog or toad's call. A very old, hoarse cat can sound croaky but it is not a typical cat noise.
Noises a cat makes.Honk: A goose sound, made loudly during migration flights to help keep the flock together in a V.
Noises a cat makes.Cluck: A hen sound. Chickens make dozens of distinct calls, and a cat cannot cluck.
Noises a cat makes.Bray: A donkey's call. It is a harsh, loud hee-haw, nothing like a cat sound.
Noises a cat makes.Bleat: A sheep or goat sound. It is not a cat noise, though a kitten's mew can sound like a tiny bleat.
Noises a cat makes.Gobble: A male turkey's call. The gobble can carry over a kilometre, making it a perfect way to attract hens.
Noises a cat makes.Ribbit: A frog sound, made famous by Hollywood. In reality only some frogs, such as the Pacific tree frog, say ribbit.

Trees.Oak: Oaks can live for centuries, and a single big tree may drop tens of thousands of acorns, which feed squirrels and jays.
Trees.Maple: Maple sap is boiled down to make syrup, and it takes around 40 liters of sap to make one liter of syrup.
Trees.Birch: Birch trees have papery white bark that peels in layers, and they're often among the first trees to colonize cleared land.
Trees.Willow: Willows grow fast along water, and their bark gave early medicine the compound that led to aspirin.
Trees.Pine: Pines keep their needles bundled in clusters, and the oldest known bristlecone pines are close to 5,000 years old.
Trees.Cedar: Cedars are aromatic conifers whose wood resists rot and moths, and the cedars of Lebanon appear on that country's flag.
Trees.Elm: Elms were once planted along streets worldwide, until Dutch elm disease, spread by bark beetles, killed millions of them.
Trees.Ash: Ash trees are now being devastated by the emerald ash borer, a beetle from Asia that has killed hundreds of millions of them in North America.
Trees.Redwood: Coast redwoods are the tallest trees on Earth, with the tallest known specimen at about 116 meters.
Trees.Baobab: The baobab can store thousands of liters of water in its swollen trunk, earning it nicknames such as the 'upside-down tree'.
Trees.Sycamore: The sycamore's flaking bark makes mottled patches of gray, brown and cream, and its winged seeds spin like helicopters.
Trees.Spruce: Spruces are cone-bearing conifers, and their wood is prized for guitars, violins and pianos because it carries sound well.
Trees.Beech: Beech trees have smooth gray bark that tempts people to carve initials, and their glossy leaves can cling on all winter.
Trees.Bamboo: Bamboo is a giant grass rather than a tree, and some species grow nearly a meter in a single day.
Trees.Banana: Banana plants look like trees, but the trunk is just tightly wrapped leaf bases, so they're technically giant herbs.
Trees.Fern: Ferns reproduce with spores rather than seeds, and they were around long before flowering plants.
Trees.Ivy: Ivy is a climbing vine, and its stems cling to walls with tiny rootlets rather than growing a trunk.
Trees.Rose: Roses are shrubs, not trees, and fossils show they grew on Earth tens of millions of years ago.
Trees.Lily: Lilies are flowering plants that grow from bulbs, and many are toxic to cats.
Trees.Sunflower: Sunflowers are annual plants, and their young heads follow the sun across the sky, but they never grow woody trunks.
Trees.Moss: Moss has no true roots or flowers, and it can survive drying out and revive when it rains.
Trees.Kelp: Kelp is a giant seaweed, not a tree, but it can grow around half a meter a day in forests under the sea.
Trees.Dandelion: A dandelion's puffball is made of fluffy seeds, and the plant is a weed whose leaves are edible.
Trees.Lavender: Lavender is a fragrant shrub, not a tree, loved by bees and used in perfumes and soaps.

Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Vegemite: A dark yeast extract spread, made from brewer's leftovers, that Australians eat thinly on buttered toast; it was launched in 1923.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Lamington: A sponge cake dipped in chocolate and rolled in coconut, which is said to be named for a Queensland governor, Lord Lamington.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Pavlova: The meringue dessert named for the ballerina Anna Pavlova is claimed by both Australia and New Zealand, and the dispute continues.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Tim Tam: A chocolate biscuit that Australians use in the 'Tim Tam slam' by sucking a hot drink through two opposite corners.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Anzac biscuit: Oats and golden syrup biscuits that were baked for soldiers in the First World War because they keep for a long time.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Fairy bread: White bread buttered and covered with hundreds and thousands, an Australian children's party staple.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Hokey pokey: A New Zealand ice cream with crunchy honeycomb toffee, and the name reportedly comes from old Italian ice cream vendors' cries.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Chiko Roll: An Australian snack created in the 1950s, a giant deep-fried roll designed to be eaten with one hand at football matches.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Weet-Bix: A wheat breakfast cereal made in both countries, which has been a pantry staple since the 1920s.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Milo: A malted chocolate drink that was developed in Australia in the 1930s, and widely beloved across Asia.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Pineapple Lumps: Chocolate-coated chewy pineapple-flavoured sweets, a New Zealand treat since the 1950s.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Poutine: A Canadian dish of fries, curds and gravy, not from Australia or New Zealand.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Haggis: A Scottish dish, though Burns Night is celebrated worldwide, including in Australia and New Zealand.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Butter tart: A small Canadian pastry, not from Australia or New Zealand.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Scotch egg: A British snack of sausage-wrapped boiled egg, not Australian or New Zealander.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Corn dog: An American fairground food, though the Australians' dagwood dog is similar.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Pierogi: Polish filled dumplings, boiled and often pan-fried, so not an Australian or New Zealand food.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Cornish pasty: An English pastry from Cornwall, though popular in Australia thanks to Cornish miners, but not Australian.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Nanaimo bar: A no-bake chocolate and custard dessert named for a city in British Columbia, so Canadian, not Australasian.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Biltong: Dried cured meat from South Africa, not Australia or New Zealand.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Bobotie: A South African spiced minced meat dish with an egg topping, not from Australasia.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Spam musubi: A Hawaiian snack of grilled Spam on rice wrapped in nori, so not Australian.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Twinkie: An American cream-filled sponge cake, not from Australia or New Zealand.
Foods from Australia or New Zealand.Hobnobs: A British oat biscuit, which is made by McVitie's, and not Australian.

Countries in Asia.Japan: It has over 6,800 islands, and vending machines selling everything from hot coffee to umbrellas on its streets.
Countries in Asia.Vietnam: It is the world's second-largest coffee exporter, after Brazil, and its S-shaped country curves along the sea.
Countries in Asia.Laos: The most heavily bombed nation per capita in history, from the Vietnam War era, and it is also a landlocked country on the Mekong.
Countries in Asia.Cambodia: Its flag shows Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world.
Countries in Asia.Nepal: It is home to Mount Everest and its flag is the only national flag that is not rectangular.
Countries in Asia.Bhutan: It measures Gross National Happiness instead of just GDP, and it is a carbon-negative country.
Countries in Asia.Bangladesh: It is one of the most densely populated large countries, and the Ganges and Brahmaputra form a huge delta there.
Countries in Asia.Mongolia: One of the least densely populated countries, with Genghis Khan's empire at one point being the largest contiguous land empire ever.
Countries in Asia.Uzbekistan: One of two doubly landlocked countries, with Silk Road cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara.
Countries in Asia.Oman: A sultanate in the southeast of Arabia, famous for frankincense, which has been traded for thousands of years.
Countries in Asia.Jordan: Petra, the rose-red city carved into rock, is here, and the Dead Sea on its border is the lowest dry land on Earth.
Countries in Asia.Malaysia: The Petronas Towers in Kuala Lumpur were the world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004.
Countries in Asia.Ethiopia: Trap: it is in Africa, and coffee comes from here, with the country using its own calendar, about seven years behind.
Countries in Asia.Somalia: Trap: it is in Africa and has the longest coastline on the African mainland.
Countries in Asia.Morocco: Trap: it is in North Africa, and Marrakech's Jemaa el-Fna square is a landmark.
Countries in Asia.Australia: Trap: it is its own continent, in Oceania rather than Asia, though it is close to Indonesia.
Countries in Asia.Madagascar: Trap: an island off Africa, and it is geologically a piece of Africa and India.
Countries in Asia.Fiji: Trap: it belongs to Oceania, a Pacific island nation.
Countries in Asia.Greece: Trap: a European country, though some of its islands lie close to Turkey.
Countries in Asia.Libya: Trap: a North African country, so not Asian.
Countries in Asia.Sudan: Trap: in Africa, the Nile's two branches meet here at Khartoum.
Countries in Asia.Tunisia: Trap: the northernmost country in Africa, though it is not Asian.
Countries in Asia.Albania: Trap: a European country in the Balkans.
Countries in Asia.Bulgaria: Trap: a European country, and it is the source of the world's oldest known worked gold treasure, found at Varna.

Mountains in the USA.Denali: At 6,190 m, it's the highest peak in North America. It was officially renamed from Mount McKinley in 2015, using its Koyukon Athabaskan name.
Mountains in the USA.Mount Whitney: At about 4,421 m, it's the highest summit in the lower 48 states, in California's Sierra Nevada. Death Valley's lowest point is only about 130 km away.
Mountains in the USA.Mount Rainier: A giant volcano near Seattle, about 4,392 m, with more glaciers than any other peak in the lower 48. It's considered a dangerous one to live beside.
Mountains in the USA.Mount St. Helens: Its eruption in May 1980 was the deadliest in US history, killing 57 people and blasting off about 400 m of the summit.
Mountains in the USA.Pikes Peak: This Colorado mountain inspired the song America the Beautiful in 1893. It's about 4,300 m high, and you can drive or take a cog railway to the top.
Mountains in the USA.Mount Hood: Oregon's tallest peak, about 3,426 m, is a dormant volcano with year-round skiing. It's visible from Portland on clear days.
Mountains in the USA.Mount Shasta: A big volcano in northern California rising about 4,300 m. It's famous in legends and spiritual lore, and it stands alone above the landscape.
Mountains in the USA.Mauna Kea: The Hawaii volcano reaches about 4,207 m above sea level, but about 10,000 m from the sea floor, which makes it taller than Everest.
Mountains in the USA.Mount Washington: The peak in New Hampshire is only about 1,917 m, yet it recorded a wind gust of 231 miles per hour in 1934, a record for a surface wind for many decades.
Mountains in the USA.Longs Peak: A famous Colorado fourteener, about 4,346 m, in Rocky Mountain National Park. It's the park's highest point.
Mountains in the USA.Grand Teton: The 4,199 m peak is the highest in Wyoming's Teton Range. The name is French for large breast, which was what trappers called the pinnacles.
Mountains in the USA.Mount Robson: The tallest peak of the Canadian Rockies, about 3,954 m, lies in British Columbia, so it's not in the USA.
Mountains in the USA.Mount Logan: Canada's highest mountain, about 5,959 m, in the Yukon. It's the second tallest in North America, but not in the USA.
Mountains in the USA.Mount Cook: New Zealand's highest peak, about 3,724 m, also known by its Maori name Aoraki. It's nowhere near the USA.
Mountains in the USA.Ben Nevis: The highest peak of the British Isles stands in Scotland, at about 1,345 m. It's a British mountain, not an American one.
Mountains in the USA.Mont Blanc: The highest peak in the Alps, at around 4,800 m, on the French-Italian border. It's not in the USA.
Mountains in the USA.Mount Kenya: Africa's second tallest, at about 5,199 m, is an extinct volcano on the equator in Kenya.
Mountains in the USA.Mount Fuji: Japan's iconic volcano, at about 3,776 m. It's in Honshu, not in the USA.
Mountains in the USA.Mount Etna: Europe's most active big volcano, in Sicily, Italy. It is not in the USA.
Mountains in the USA.Mount Elbrus: At about 5,642 m, it's the highest mountain in Russia and often called Europe's highest, in the Caucasus.
Mountains in the USA.Matterhorn: A famous peak on the Swiss-Italian border. A copy of it is a ride at Disneyland in California, but the real one isn't in the USA.
Mountains in the USA.Mount Kosciuszko: Australia's highest mainland peak, at about 2,228 m. It was named by a Polish explorer for a Polish hero, and it's not in the USA.
Mountains in the USA.Popocatépetl: An active volcano in Mexico, about 5,400 m, near Mexico City. Its name means smoking mountain in Nahuatl.
Mountains in the USA.Mount Teide: Spain's highest peak, about 3,715 m, is a volcano on Tenerife in the Canary Islands. It's not in the USA.

Sedimentary rocks.Sandstone: Cemented grains of sand, often showing ancient dune layers. Petra's rose-red facades in Jordan and Uluru in Australia are both sandstone.
Sedimentary rocks.Limestone: Built mostly from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures, it can hold fossils. The Great Pyramid was clad in polished white limestone.
Sedimentary rocks.Shale: Hardened mud that splits into thin layers. Famous fossil beds, such as the Burgess Shale, preserve soft-bodied creatures in it.
Sedimentary rocks.Chalk: Made of microscopic algae plates called coccoliths piled on ancient seabeds. The White Cliffs of Dover are chalk.
Sedimentary rocks.Coal: Compressed ancient swamp plants from the Carboniferous period. Surprisingly, it is a sedimentary rock, not a mineral, since it has no fixed crystal structure.
Sedimentary rocks.Conglomerate: Rounded pebbles cemented in finer material, a bit like natural concrete. The rounding shows the pebbles were tumbled by water first.
Sedimentary rocks.Mudstone: Hardened mud, a close relative of shale that does not split into layers. Dinosaur footprints are sometimes preserved in it.
Sedimentary rocks.Siltstone: Between mudstone and sandstone, it's made of grains finer than sand but coarser than clay.
Sedimentary rocks.Flint: A hard, glassy rock that forms as nodules in chalk. Stone Age toolmakers chipped it into sharp blades, and it throws sparks against steel.
Sedimentary rocks.Rock salt: Left behind when ancient seas evaporated, it forms thick underground beds. Some of it is mined to salt winter roads.
Sedimentary rocks.Travertine: Deposited by hot springs that are rich in dissolved limestone. Rome used it for the Colosseum and St. Peter's colonnades.
Sedimentary rocks.Granite: A trap: it's igneous, formed when magma cooled slowly underground, so its crystals are large and visible.
Sedimentary rocks.Basalt: A trap: igneous, from lava that cooled quickly. It forms most of the ocean floor.
Sedimentary rocks.Obsidian: A trap: igneous, a natural glass from rapidly cooled lava. It has no crystals, so it breaks with razor edges.
Sedimentary rocks.Pumice: A trap: it's igneous, frothy lava that hardened full of bubbles. It floats on water.
Sedimentary rocks.Marble: A trap: metamorphic, limestone transformed by heat and pressure. It comes from sedimentary rock but is no longer one.
Sedimentary rocks.Slate: A trap: it's metamorphic, shale changed by heat and pressure. It cleaves into thin flat sheets.
Sedimentary rocks.Gneiss: A trap: metamorphic, with stripy bands from intense heat and pressure. Some is among the oldest rock on Earth.
Sedimentary rocks.Schist: A trap: metamorphic, shiny with mica flakes. Its layered sparkle shows it was squeezed and heated deep underground.
Sedimentary rocks.Quartzite: A trap: sandstone that has been metamorphosed into a tougher rock whose grains have fused.
Sedimentary rocks.Gabbro: A trap: it's igneous, made of slowly cooled magma. It's dark, coarse, and chemically like basalt.
Sedimentary rocks.Diorite: A trap: it's igneous, not sedimentary, cooled slowly from magma underground. Its black-and-white speckled look resembles salt and pepper.
Sedimentary rocks.Soapstone: A trap: metamorphic and rich in soft talc. Not sedimentary, despite how easily it carves.
Sedimentary rocks.Andesite: A trap: igneous, not sedimentary. Named for the Andes mountains, it forms from volcanoes above subduction zones.

Carnivorous plants.Venus flytrap: It snaps shut only if two trigger hairs are touched within about 20 seconds, which avoids wasting energy on raindrops. It grows wild only in the Carolinas.
Carnivorous plants.Pitcher plant: Its slippery, tube-shaped leaves fill with digestive fluid. Insects slip in and drown, and the plant absorbs nutrients from them.
Carnivorous plants.Sundew: Sticky, glistening droplets on its tentacle-like hairs trap insects. Darwin studied sundews closely and called them wonderful plants.
Carnivorous plants.Bladderwort: Its underwater traps fire in about a millisecond, among the fastest movements in the plant world. They suck in tiny water creatures.
Carnivorous plants.Butterwort: Its leaves are coated with sticky mucilage that traps small insects. In Scandinavia, its leaves were once used to curdle milk into a stretchy yogurt.
Carnivorous plants.Cobra lily: A pitcher plant of Oregon and California named for a hooded tube like a cobra's head. Water cooled by the plant's roots protects it in summer.
Carnivorous plants.Monkey cup: The Nepenthes pitcher plant. Some giant species trap rats, and one Borneo type has a pitcher that tree shrews use as a toilet.
Carnivorous plants.Waterwheel plant: A floating, rootless relative of the Venus flytrap, with snap traps arranged like spokes of a wheel to catch tiny aquatic prey.
Carnivorous plants.Trumpet pitcher: Sarracenia, the trumpet-shaped pitcher plants of the American southeast. Some release a scent to attract insects, then trap them in a slippery tube.
Carnivorous plants.Snapdragon: A trap: its 'jaws' only look like they snap. Bees pry the flower open to pollinate it, and nothing gets eaten.
Carnivorous plants.Tiger lily: Its orange, spotted petals are only for show. It grows from a bulb, and the bulbs have been eaten in parts of Asia.
Carnivorous plants.Cactus: Cacti collect their food by photosynthesis alone, and their spines are modified leaves that cut water loss. None are carnivorous.
Carnivorous plants.Aloe vera: A succulent that stores water in thick leaves. It is not a meat eater, and its gel is the part used in skin care.
Carnivorous plants.Spider plant: A popular houseplant that sends out dangling baby plantlets. It looks like a creature but eats no insects.
Carnivorous plants.Fly agaric: A red-and-white toadstool that has been used to kill flies, hence its name. As a fungus, it is not a plant at all.
Carnivorous plants.Catnip: A mint relative whose chemical nepetalactone affects about two-thirds of cats. It grows by sunlight, not by trapping prey.
Carnivorous plants.Snake plant: A tough houseplant also called mother-in-law's tongue. It is not carnivorous, but it can survive weeks of neglect.
Carnivorous plants.Dragon fruit: The fruit of a climbing cactus that blooms at night. Its flowers are pollinated by bats and moths, not by catching bugs.
Carnivorous plants.Mimosa: Touch a leaf and it folds up in seconds. It looks as if it's reacting to prey, but the movement just discourages grazers.
Carnivorous plants.Bird of paradise: Its flower looks like a colorful bird's head. It makes nectar for sunbirds to pollinate it, not traps for insects.
Carnivorous plants.Lion's mane: A trap: it is a shaggy edible mushroom, so a fungus. The largest lion's mane known is a jellyfish with tentacles over 30 meters long.
Carnivorous plants.Wolfsbane: Also called monkshood, and deadly poisonous. Poison defends it against being eaten rather than helping it to eat.
Carnivorous plants.Foxglove: The source of the heart drug digoxin, and toxic in raw form. Bees climb into its tubular flowers, and it traps nothing.
Carnivorous plants.Stinging nettle: Its hairs inject a burning mix of chemicals as defense. Even so, it is no meat-eater, and cooked nettles make a good soup.

Characters in The Lion King.Simba: 'Simba' is Swahili for lion, and the cub's story is often compared to Hamlet.
Characters in The Lion King.Mufasa: James Earl Jones voiced the king, and also Darth Vader, which makes him one of the most famous voices in film.
Characters in The Lion King.Scar: Jeremy Irons voiced the lion's scheming uncle, and his drawl is a perfect villain voice.
Characters in The Lion King.Nala: Her name is Swahili for 'gift', and she's Simba's childhood friend who convinces him to return.
Characters in The Lion King.Timon: The meerkat's 'hakuna matata' philosophy is Swahili for 'no worries', and he was voiced by Nathan Lane in the 1994 film.
Characters in The Lion King.Pumbaa: His name is Swahili for 'simpleton', and the warthog's gas jokes ensured his place in the hearts of children.
Characters in The Lion King.Rafiki: The mandrill shaman's name means 'friend' in Swahili, and he lifts Simba up on Pride Rock at the start.
Characters in The Lion King.Zazu: The hornbill, Mufasa's advisor, was voiced by Rowan Atkinson, who's better known as Mr. Bean.
Characters in The Lion King.Sarabi: Simba's mother, the lioness leading the pride under Scar, has a name that means 'mirage' in Swahili.
Characters in The Lion King.Shenzi: The leader of the hyena trio was voiced by Whoopi Goldberg in the 1994 film.
Characters in The Lion King.Banzai: The hyena who says 'Mufasa?' was voiced by Cheech Marin, a comedian best known for the duo Cheech & Chong.
Characters in The Lion King.Bambi: Bambi is a deer from Disney's 1942 film, not the Pride Lands.
Characters in The Lion King.Baloo: Baloo is the bear from The Jungle Book, not the Pride Lands.
Characters in The Lion King.Bagheera: Bagheera is the black panther of The Jungle Book, not The Lion King.
Characters in The Lion King.Shere Khan: Shere Khan is the tiger of The Jungle Book, a different story from The Lion King.
Characters in The Lion King.Kaa: Kaa is the snake of The Jungle Book, not the Pride Lands.
Characters in The Lion King.Alex: Alex is the lion of DreamWorks' Madagascar, voiced by Ben Stiller, not Simba's pride.
Characters in The Lion King.Marty: Marty is the zebra of Madagascar, a DreamWorks film, not The Lion King.
Characters in The Lion King.Gloria: Gloria is the hippo of Madagascar, not The Lion King.
Characters in The Lion King.Melman: Melman is the giraffe of Madagascar, not The Lion King.
Characters in The Lion King.Diego: Diego is the saber-toothed cat of Ice Age, not The Lion King.
Characters in The Lion King.Manny: Manny is the mammoth of Ice Age, not The Lion King.
Characters in The Lion King.Thumper: Thumper is the rabbit from Bambi, not The Lion King.
Characters in The Lion King.Tai Lung: Tai Lung is the snow leopard of DreamWorks' Kung Fu Panda, not The Lion King.

Characters in Moana.Moana: The title heroine's name means ocean, and Moana is a Polynesian wayfinder who sails beyond her reef.
Characters in Moana.Maui: Maui is a demigod from Polynesian myth, voiced by Dwayne Johnson, with hand-animated tattoos, including a tiny Mini Maui.
Characters in Moana.Heihei: Heihei is a not-very-bright rooster who eats rocks, and he is one of Disney's silliest sidekicks.
Characters in Moana.Pua: Pua is Moana's pet pig, and the name means flower in Hawaiian.
Characters in Moana.Tamatoa: Tamatoa is a giant coconut crab who collects shiny things, and Jemaine Clement voices him with David Bowie flair.
Characters in Moana.Te Fiti: Te Fiti is the island goddess whose stolen heart sets the story going, and the island itself is her body.
Characters in Moana.Te Ka: Te Ka is a lava demon who turns out to be Te Fiti's corrupted form after her heart was stolen.
Characters in Moana.Gramma Tala: Gramma Tala is Moana's grandmother who becomes a manta ray in spirit; Rachel House voices her.
Characters in Moana.Chief Tui: Chief Tui is Moana's father, voiced by Temuera Morrison, who also played Jango Fett in Star Wars.
Characters in Moana.Sina: Sina is Moana's mother, who supports her daughter's dreams even when her father opposes them.
Characters in Moana.Kakamora: The Kakamora are tiny coconut pirates, based on Melanesian myths of small, hairy beings from the Solomon Islands.
Characters in Moana.Lilo: Lilo is a Hawaiian girl from Lilo & Stitch, a different Disney film from Moana.
Characters in Moana.Stitch: Stitch is Experiment 626, the blue alien from the Hawaii-set Lilo & Stitch, not Moana.
Characters in Moana.Nani: Nani is Lilo's older sister who struggles to keep their family together in Lilo & Stitch.
Characters in Moana.Jumba: Jumba is the alien scientist who built Stitch, so he is part of the Lilo & Stitch cast, not Moana.
Characters in Moana.Pleakley: Pleakley is the one-eyed alien who thinks he's an Earth expert, in Lilo & Stitch.
Characters in Moana.Raya: Raya is the heroine of Raya and the Last Dragon, which is inspired by Southeast Asian cultures.
Characters in Moana.Sisu: Sisu is the water dragon in Raya and the Last Dragon, not Moana.
Characters in Moana.Namaari: Namaari is the princess of Fang in Raya and the Last Dragon, a rival turned ally.
Characters in Moana.Mulan: Mulan is a Chinese warrior who disguises herself as a man, and she has her own film.
Characters in Moana.Mushu: Mushu is the small dragon guardian voiced by Eddie Murphy in Mulan, not Moana.
Characters in Moana.Li Shang: Li Shang is the captain and love interest in Mulan, not part of Moana's story.
Characters in Moana.Pocahontas: Pocahontas is from the 1995 film and sings 'Colors of the Wind', which won an Oscar.
Characters in Moana.Meeko: Meeko is Pocahontas's mischievous raccoon friend who steals the food of travelers.

Film score composers.John Williams: He scored Star Wars, Jaws, Indiana Jones and Harry Potter, and has been nominated for over 50 Oscars, more than any living person.
Film score composers.Hans Zimmer: The German composer scored Inception, The Dark Knight and Dune. He famously blends orchestra with synthesizers.
Film score composers.Ennio Morricone: The Italian maestro scored Sergio Leone's Westerns, including The Good, the Bad and the Ugly. He finally won a competitive Oscar in 2016.
Film score composers.Howard Shore: He composed the Lord of the Rings trilogy. The Canadian won three Oscars for the three films.
Film score composers.Danny Elfman: Once the singer of Oingo Boingo, he scored Tim Burton films and wrote The Simpsons' theme tune.
Film score composers.James Horner: He scored Titanic and Braveheart, and the Titanic song My Heart Will Go On came from his melody. He died in a plane crash in 2015.
Film score composers.Alan Menken: The man behind the Disney Renaissance scores, including The Little Mermaid and Beauty and the Beast. He's won eight Oscars.
Film score composers.Michael Giacchino: He scored Up, The Incredibles and Lost. His Up score won him an Oscar in 2010.
Film score composers.Bernard Herrmann: He scored Psycho with only strings, giving the shower scene its shrieking violins. Hitchcock first wanted no music there.
Film score composers.John Barry: The English composer shaped the sound of James Bond and wrote the score for Out of Africa and Dances with Wolves.
Film score composers.Ludwig Göransson: The Swedish composer scored Black Panther and Oppenheimer, and won an Oscar for each. He also worked with Childish Gambino.
Film score composers.Thomas Newman: He scored Shawshank Redemption, American Beauty, and Skyfall. His family includes Randy Newman, his cousin.
Film score composers.Alexandre Desplat: The French composer scored The Grand Budapest Hotel and The Shape of Water and won Oscars for both.
Film score composers.Steven Spielberg: A director, not a composer. His partnership with John Williams stretches across about 30 films since the 1970s.
Film score composers.Christopher Nolan: A director who works with Hans Zimmer. Nolan's films are known for scores woven closely into the sound design.
Film score composers.Tim Burton: A director, not a composer. His long partnership with Danny Elfman created gothic scores for Beetlejuice and Edward Scissorhands.
Film score composers.James Cameron: He directed Titanic and Avatar but didn't compose. James Horner wrote his scores for Titanic and Aliens.
Film score composers.Peter Jackson: He directed the Lord of the Rings trilogy while Howard Shore wrote the music. He's a director, not a composer.
Film score composers.Quentin Tarantino: The director is famous for using existing songs rather than original scores. Ennio Morricone did write one for The Hateful Eight.
Film score composers.Sergio Leone: The Italian director of spaghetti Westerns. His friendship with composer Ennio Morricone started in school.
Film score composers.Alfred Hitchcock: The suspense director worked with Bernard Herrmann on several films. He's a director, not a composer.
Film score composers.George Lucas: He made Star Wars but not its music. He asked John Williams for a Holst-inspired, classical sound.
Film score composers.Ridley Scott: The director of Alien and Gladiator. He worked with Hans Zimmer on Gladiator, and he isn't a composer.
Film score composers.Martin Scorsese: A director with a famous music taste, he usually picks existing songs. He isn't a composer.

Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Athens: The modern Games began here in 1896, and the city hosted again in 2004, bringing the Olympics back to their birthplace.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Stockholm: The 1912 Games pioneered electronic timing and photo-finish equipment at the Olympics, and they included the modern pentathlon's debut.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Antwerp: The 1920 Games saw the Olympic flag with five rings appear for the first time, and the oath was first taken here.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Amsterdam: The 1928 Games introduced the Olympic flame in a tower, and women were allowed to compete in track and field for the first time.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Helsinki: The 1952 Games marked the Soviet Union's Olympic debut, and the city had lost its planned 1940 Games to the outbreak of war.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Melbourne: In 1956 these were the first Games in the Southern Hemisphere, and athletes first mingled together at the closing ceremony, not by nation.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Rome: In 1960 the marathon ended at the Arch of Constantine, and Abebe Bikila of Ethiopia won it running barefoot.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Mexico City: At about 2,240 meters, thin air at the 1968 Games helped Bob Beamon leap 8.90 meters, a record that stood for 23 years.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Montreal: Nadia Comaneci scored the first perfect ten in Olympic gymnastics in 1976, and the scoreboard could only show 1.00.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Seoul: The 1988 Games marked the return of full participation, after boycotts in 1980 and 1984, and Ben Johnson lost his 100m gold to doping.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Barcelona: The 1992 Games opened with an archer lighting the flame by shooting a burning arrow, and the Dream Team made its debut.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Atlanta: The 1996 Games marked the centennial, and Muhammad Ali lit the cauldron to a roar.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Sydney: In 2000, Cathy Freeman lit the flame and won the 400m gold, and the Games are often rated among the best.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Chicago: It was among the finalists for 2016 but was eliminated first, with Rio winning the vote.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Madrid: The Spanish capital bid several times, including for 2012, 2016 and 2020, but never won the vote.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Istanbul: The city bid for 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012 and 2020 but never won, the most bids without success.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Toronto: The Canadian city bid for the 1996 and 2008 Games and lost both, while Montreal hosted in 1976.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Cape Town: The South African city bid for 2004, but Athens won, so Africa has never hosted a Summer Games.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.New York: Bids for 2012 failed in the final rounds, and the city has never hosted either Games.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Calgary: This Canadian city hosted the 1988 Winter Games, not the Summer ones.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Sochi: The 2014 Winter Olympics happened here on the Black Sea, so it's a Winter host, not a Summer one.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Lillehammer: A small Norwegian town hosted the Winter Games in 1994, and has never hosted the Summer Games.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Vancouver: The city hosted the Winter Olympics in 2010, not a Summer Games.
Cities that have hosted the Summer Olymp.Cairo: Egypt's capital bid for 2008 but never won, so Africa still waits for its first Summer Games.

Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Bingo: Descends from an Italian lottery of the 1500s. The name bingo arrived in 1920s America.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Eyes down: The caller's traditional opener, Eyes down, look in, tells players to focus on their cards before the first number.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Legs eleven: The number 11, which looks like two legs standing. Callers often get a cheeky wolf whistle.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Two little ducks: The number 22, which resembles two ducks floating. Players often quack back.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Clickety click: The number 66, because the repeated sixes sound like a rapid click. Callers often add the rhyme with a flourish.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Full house: Covering every number on your ticket wins the top prize. Poker uses the same phrase for a pair plus three of a kind.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.House: In the UK you can shout house instead of bingo when your card is full, from housey-housey, an old name for the game.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Kelly's eye: The number 1. The origin may be old military slang, probably referencing an eye.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Unlucky for some: The number 13, said with a wince, as superstition makes 13 a number to avoid.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Top of the shop: The number 90, the highest ball in 90-ball bingo, hence the top of the card shop.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Line: The first prize: complete one horizontal line, then two lines, then a full house.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Checkmate: The chess finish, from Persian shah mat. In bingo you shout bingo or house, and the king never gets trapped.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Fore: A golfer's warning shout when a ball is flying toward others on the course, not a bingo call.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Yahtzee: Shouted when you roll five of a kind in the dice game, which is named for a yacht, not bingo.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Uno: Called in the card game when you're down to your last card, not a bingo call.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Snap: Shouted in the card game when two matching cards appear, a quick-reflex cry rather than a bingo one.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Gin: Gin rummy's call when your hand has no unmatched cards, and not something you'd hear at bingo.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Timber: A lumberjack's warning that a tree is about to fall, long before bingo existed.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Strike: Bowling's all-pins-down result, a celebration of a different kind from yelling bingo.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Jinx: Said when two people speak the same word at once, a playground courtesy rather than a bingo call.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Howzat: A cricket appeal to the umpire for a dismissal, short for How's that?
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Goal: The football cry when the ball hits the net, not something you shout over a bingo ticket.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Check: Chess's warning that a king is under attack, and not a bingo call.
Calls you'd hear at a UK bingo hall.Touchdown: American football's six-point score, a cry from the gridiron rather than the bingo hall.

Things thrown as part of their sport.Javelin: Jan Zelezny's 98.48 m throw in 1996 is still the world record. The men's javelin is about 2.6 m long.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Discus: The ancient Greek statue Discobolus shows a thrower mid-spin. Modern men's discs weigh 2 kg.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Shot: A 7.26 kg metal ball for men, technically pushed or put rather than thrown, from the shoulder.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Hammer: A 7.26 kg ball on a wire, thrown from a cage. Yuriy Sedykh's 86.74 m from 1986 still stands.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Caber: A tree trunk about six metres long, tossed end over end at Scottish Highland games. Judges score by clock position.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Frisbee: The name is said to come from Frisbie Pie Company tins that Yale students threw around.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Dart: A perfect leg in 501 is nine darts, a feat so rare that players treasure it.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Horseshoe: Ringers score the most. The sport is pitched at 40 feet in the open class.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Boomerang: The oldest known boomerang, found in a cave in Poland, is about 30,000 years old, though it was not a returning kind.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Cornhole bag: Bags were originally filled with corn kernels, now often resin pellets, and are tossed at a board 27 feet away.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Dodgeball: Unlike most sports, the thrown ball targets people rather than a goal, hitting opponents to remove them.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Puck: A hockey puck is struck with a stick and slides at over 100 mph, rather than being thrown.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Shuttlecock: Badminton's shuttlecock is hit with a racket and can fly at over 200 mph in smashes, but never thrown.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Golf ball: A golf ball is struck with a club, never thrown. The dimples reduce drag and let it travel farther.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Pool ball: Pool balls are struck with a cue, never thrown, and a thrown one would lose you the match at once.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Racket: A racket is swung to hit, not thrown. Tossing it in anger can earn a code violation, as in tennis.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Baseball bat: A bat is swung to hit, and throwing it can get a player ejected. Not thrown as part of the sport.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Oar: An oar is pulled through the water by rowers, never thrown, though cox's megaphones sometimes are.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Saddle: A saddle is something you sit on in equestrian sport, never something you toss.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Hockey stick: A hockey stick is swung to hit the puck, and throwing it at someone is a penalty.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Tee: A tee is pushed into the ground to hold a golf ball for the first shot of a hole.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Cue: A cue is used to strike a ball in pool or snooker, nothing like a throw.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Croquet ball: A croquet ball is struck with a mallet through hoops, not thrown, and the game dates to the 1800s.
Things thrown as part of their sport.Skis: Skis are worn on the feet and carry skiers down hills. Not thrown, except by a tumbling skier.

Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Chariot racing: Teams of four horses raced around turning posts, and wrecks were so common that few chariots usually finished.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Wrestling: Matches were decided by three throws, and wrestlers oiled their skin, then dusted it with fine sand to get a grip.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Boxing: Fighters wrapped leather thongs around their fists, and with no rounds or weight classes, a bout ran until someone gave up.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Pankration: A brutal blend of boxing and wrestling where only biting and eye-gouging were banned: the ancient world's version of MMA.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Javelin: Throwers looped a leather strap called an ankyle around the shaft, which added spin and stability to the throw.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Discus: Myron's Discobolus statue froze a thrower mid-spin; the bronze original is lost, and Roman marble copies are what survive.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Long jump: Jumpers swung stone or lead weights called halteres forward in mid-air, which helped carry them farther.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Footrace: The stadion, a sprint of about 190 meters, was the oldest event, and its track gave us the word stadium.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Pentathlon: One contest combining a sprint, long jump, discus, javelin and wrestling, with the all-round champion earning huge prestige.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Horse racing: Riders had no saddles or stirrups, and the olive wreath went to the horse's owner, not the jockey.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Race in armor: Runners sprinted in helmet and greaves carrying a heavy shield, and this race closed the Games' program.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Marathon: Not an ancient event: the marathon was invented for the 1896 Athens Games to honor the legend of Pheidippides' run.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Swimming: The Greeks could swim, but no event existed at Olympia; swimming debuted at the modern Games in 1896.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Gymnastics: The word means exercising naked in Greek, yet it was no Olympic event then; gymnastics joined the modern Games in 1896.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Fencing: Ancient combat sports were unarmed, so no swords; fencing is a modern sport that joined the 1896 Olympics.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Tennis: A medieval invention that joined the Olympics in 1896, vanished after 1924, then came back in 1988.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Pole vault: Vaulting with a pole began as a way to cross Dutch canals and ditches; it was never an ancient Olympic event.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.High jump: Ancient Olympia had a long jump but no high jump; the modern event took shape in 19th-century Britain.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Shot put: Not ancient: ancient stone-throwing contests used a discus, and the shot put grew out of tossing cannonballs in Britain.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Cycling: The bicycle arrived in the 1800s, so ancient champions never raced one; cycling was on the very first modern program in 1896.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Rowing: The Greeks were master sailors, but nobody rowed at Olympia; rowing was planned for 1896 but was cancelled by rough seas.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Hammer throw: A tradition of Celtic and Highland games, it joined the Olympics only in 1900 and was not an ancient event.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Volleyball: Volleyball was invented in 1895 in Massachusetts by William Morgan and became Olympic in 1964, far later than the ancient Games.
Events at the ancient Olympic Games.Relay race: Relay racing is modern; the torch relay to light the Games was invented for the 1936 Berlin Olympics, not by the Greeks.

Things you can sharpen.Pencil: Sharpening a pencil often makes it shorter by about a centimeter or more, which is why a new one is far longer than a worn one.
Things you can sharpen.Knife: A honing steel doesn't remove much metal, it realigns a knife's edge, which bends over slightly with use.
Things you can sharpen.Scissors: Scissors are sharpened by running the beveled edge on a stone, and some people even snip aluminum foil as a quick fix.
Things you can sharpen.Axe: A well-sharpened axe cuts clean through the wood fibers, and a dull one just bounces and is more likely to cause an accident.
Things you can sharpen.Ice skates: Skates are usually sharpened with a shallow groove between two edges, and the hollow depth is chosen to suit the skater's style.
Things you can sharpen.Chisel: A woodworker's chisel is often sharpened to a bevel angle of about 25 degrees, then honed to a mirror shine.
Things you can sharpen.Lawnmower blade: A dull blade tears grass instead of cutting it, and torn tips turn brown, so mowers sharpen blades once a year.
Things you can sharpen.Eyeliner pencil: A soft eyeliner pencil is sharpened in a tiny sharpener, and chilling it first in the fridge helps it cut clean.
Things you can sharpen.Crayon: Crayons can be sharpened with a special sharpener, and many pencil sharpeners have a hole for the thick ones.
Things you can sharpen.Machete: A machete is a big, broad blade that is typically sharpened with a file, and it is used to clear thick brush.
Things you can sharpen.Garden shears: Pruning shears with dull edges crush stems rather than cut them, which can let disease into the plant.
Things you can sharpen.Spoon: A spoon has a rounded edge, and trying to sharpen it would do little good.
Things you can sharpen.Hammer: A hammer works by weight and has no edge to sharpen, as the face of the head is meant to be flat and tough.
Things you can sharpen.Paintbrush: A paintbrush's tip is shaped by its bristles, and it can't be sharpened, though a good one comes to a fine point.
Things you can sharpen.Pen: A pen has a tip that feeds ink, so it can't be sharpened, unlike a pencil whose point wears away.
Things you can sharpen.Marker: A marker's tip is a felt or fiber nib, and sharpening it would only wreck it.
Things you can sharpen.Eraser: An eraser is rubber and wears down as it works, and a sharp corner can be made by cutting with a knife, but it isn't sharpened.
Things you can sharpen.Ruler: A ruler is a straight edge, and a sharp one would be a hazard, not a feature.
Things you can sharpen.Broom: A broom's bristles wear down with use, and there's no way to sharpen them.
Things you can sharpen.Sponge: A sponge is soft and porous, and sharpening it makes no sense.
Things you can sharpen.Ladle: A ladle has a rounded bowl for scooping soup, and no edge to sharpen.
Things you can sharpen.Highlighter: A highlighter has a chisel-shaped felt tip, but it can't be sharpened, and it is worn down by writing.
Things you can sharpen.Toothbrush: Its bristles are soft nylon, and a sharp one would hurt your gums, which makes sharpening pointless.
Things you can sharpen.Whisk: A whisk is a set of wire loops for beating, and a sharp edge would just damage the bowl.

Parts of a pen.Nib: The nib's tiny slit pulls ink down by capillary action, the same effect that draws water up a paper towel.
Parts of a pen.Ink cartridge: Cartridges made fountain pens far less messy. They were popularized in the mid-1900s as an alternative to filling from a bottle.
Parts of a pen.Cap: The small hole near the top of many pen caps is there so a swallowed cap lets air through, a safety design against choking.
Parts of a pen.Clip: The clip keeps the pen in a pocket, but it also stops a round pen from rolling off a desk.
Parts of a pen.Barrel: The barrel is the main body you hold. Pen makers use everything from resin to metal to carved wood for it.
Parts of a pen.Spring: A small spring inside a click pen pushes the refill back and forth. It is the part that makes the satisfying click.
Parts of a pen.Ball tip: A ballpoint's tiny rolling ball is often made of tungsten carbide, and it's usually under a millimeter across. It rolls ink onto the paper.
Parts of a pen.Clicker: The clicker button works with a cam mechanism that alternately locks and releases the refill. Many people find the click irresistible.
Parts of a pen.Grip: The grip, the part where fingers rest, is often rubber or textured plastic to cut hand fatigue during long writing.
Parts of a pen.Lead: Pencils contain this, not pens. Despite the name, a pencil's 'lead' has no actual lead; it's graphite mixed with clay.
Parts of a pen.Graphite: Graphite is the pencil's marking material, and it's the same carbon form that diamond is not. Pens use liquid ink instead.
Parts of a pen.Ferrule: This small metal band holds a pencil's eraser. It has no place on a pen.
Parts of a pen.Wick: Wicks belong in candles and oil lamps. A pen's ink flows without one, thanks to a felt reservoir or a ball tip.
Parts of a pen.Bristles: Bristles belong to brushes. Pens write with a nib or ball tip, not hair or fiber.
Parts of a pen.Lens: A lens belongs to a camera or glasses. Pens have none, although some novelty pens hide a tiny one.
Parts of a pen.Blade: Blades belong to knives and scissors. A pen aims to write, not cut.
Parts of a pen.Sole: A sole is on the bottom of a shoe or foot. It has no counterpart in a pen.
Parts of a pen.Lace: Laces tie shoes. A pen has nothing to tie, though a lanyard hole is sometimes added.
Parts of a pen.Wheel: Wheels turn vehicles and some mouse devices. A pen has only a tiny rolling ball, which isn't a true wheel.
Parts of a pen.Spout: A spout pours liquid from kettles and jugs. A pen releases ink in a thin controlled line, not a pour.
Parts of a pen.Hinge: Hinges are on doors and laptops. A typical pen has no hinge, only a push or twist mechanism.
Parts of a pen.Antenna: Antennas receive signals on radios and phones. A pen has no radio parts unless it's a smart pen.
Parts of a pen.Keyhole: A keyhole is part of a lock. Pens don't have one, though a pen can be used to pick a bad lock in movies.
Parts of a pen.Lampshade: A lampshade diffuses a bulb's light. A pen has no bulb, though some novelty pens have a tiny light.

Minerals your body needs.Calcium: About 99 percent of your calcium is stored in bones and teeth, and the rest helps muscles and nerves work.
Minerals your body needs.Iron: Iron lets red blood cells carry oxygen, and deficiency is the most common nutritional shortfall in the world.
Minerals your body needs.Zinc: Zinc supports immunity and wound healing, and your body can't store much, so you need a steady supply.
Minerals your body needs.Magnesium: Magnesium helps hundreds of enzyme reactions and steadies muscles and heartbeat. Nuts and greens are good sources.
Minerals your body needs.Potassium: Potassium balances fluids and keeps your heartbeat steady, and bananas are famous for it but potatoes beat them.
Minerals your body needs.Sodium: Sodium helps nerves fire, but most people eat far more salt than needed, which raises blood pressure.
Minerals your body needs.Iodine: Your thyroid needs iodine, which is why table salt in many countries is iodized to prevent goiter.
Minerals your body needs.Phosphorus: Phosphorus is the second most abundant mineral in your body and forms part of both bone and DNA.
Minerals your body needs.Selenium: Needed only in trace amounts, selenium protects cells, and a single Brazil nut can supply a day's worth.
Minerals your body needs.Copper: Copper helps your body use iron and make connective tissue, and the adult body holds only about 70 milligrams.
Minerals your body needs.Manganese: Manganese aids bone formation and metabolism, and you need only a few milligrams a day from nuts and grains.
Minerals your body needs.Vitamin C: A trap: vitamin C is organic, so it's a vitamin, not a mineral, though both are essential nutrients.
Minerals your body needs.Niacin: Niacin is vitamin B3, an organic compound, and its deficiency causes the disease pellagra.
Minerals your body needs.Folate: Folate is a B vitamin, not a mineral, and it helps prevent birth defects of the spine.
Minerals your body needs.Lead: Lead is a toxic metal with no known role in the body, harmful especially to children's developing brains.
Minerals your body needs.Mercury: Mercury is a poison, building up in large fish like swordfish, and has no useful job in your body.
Minerals your body needs.Arsenic: Arsenic is famously poisonous, though tiny traces occur naturally in some foods like rice.
Minerals your body needs.Protein: Protein is a macronutrient, built from amino acids, rather than a mineral.
Minerals your body needs.Fiber: Fiber is plant carbohydrate rather than a mineral, and it feeds the bacteria in your gut.
Minerals your body needs.Caffeine: Caffeine is an organic stimulant and not a mineral, and your body needs none of it.
Minerals your body needs.Biotin: Biotin is vitamin B7, an organic nutrient, so it isn't a mineral despite appearing in hair supplements.
Minerals your body needs.Glucose: Glucose is a simple sugar your cells burn for energy, not a mineral.
Minerals your body needs.Cholesterol: Cholesterol is a waxy fat your liver makes, and it's used to build cell membranes, not an element.
Minerals your body needs.Uranium: Uranium is a radioactive heavy metal with no biological use, and trace amounts in water are harmful, not beneficial.

Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Cardiac: The adjective for anything related to the heart, as in cardiac arrest, which is when the heart stops pumping effectively.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Cardiology: The branch of medicine devoted to the heart and blood vessels, from the Greek 'kardia'.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Cardiologist: A heart specialist, often using ECGs and echocardiograms, which use sound waves to picture the heart.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Cardiovascular: This blends heart and 'vascular' for blood vessels, and cardiovascular disease is the world's leading cause of death.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Electrocardiogram: An ECG records the heart's electrical activity, a technique that began with Willem Einthoven's early 1900s work.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Tachycardia: A resting heart rate over 100 beats per minute, from Greek 'tachys' meaning fast.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Bradycardia: A slow heartbeat under 60 per minute, normal for athletes yet worrying in others, from Greek 'bradys' for slow.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Myocardium: This is the heart's muscle layer, whose name combines Greek for muscle and heart, and it is the thickest layer.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Pericardium: A tough double-layered sac around the heart that cushions it, and 'peri' means around.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Cardiomyopathy: A disease of the heart muscle that makes it harder to pump blood, and it can be inherited.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Endocarditis: An infection of the heart's inner lining and valves, and 'endo' means within.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Cardiogram: The suffix -gram means a recording, so a cardiogram is a written trace of heartbeats, the shorter cousin of electrocardiogram.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Cardigan: A trap: cardigan has no link to hearts. It's named after the 7th Earl of Cardigan, a British Army officer.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Cardinal: Cardinal comes from Latin 'cardo' meaning hinge, so a cardinal is a pivotal person, with nothing about hearts.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Cardboard: The 'card' in cardboard traces back to a Greek word for papyrus sheet, a paper root, unrelated to the Greek word for heart.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Cardamom: This fragrant spice is a seed pod from the ginger family and ranks among the costliest spices, and it has nothing to do with hearts.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Cartilage: Cartilage shares the 'car' start only by coincidence, coming from Latin 'cartilago' and not Greek for heart.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Carnival: Carnival probably comes from Latin 'carne vale', 'farewell to meat', and has no heart in it.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Cartography: Cartography is map-making, from Greek 'chartes' meaning papyrus sheet.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Cartoon: A cartoon was originally a full-size drawing for a painting, from Italian 'cartone', a large sheet of paper.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Discard: Discard hides 'card' in the playing-card sense, as in tossing a card away, so it only looks like it's from 'cardio'.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Credit card: The 'card' here is a plastic or paper card, from a word for paper, while 'cardio' is Greek for heart.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Cardiff: Cardiff is the capital of Wales, and its name has no relation to the heart.
Words built on 'cardio' (heart).Recording: Trap with a twist: 'record' really does come from Latin for 'heart', since to record was to bring back to heart, but it holds no 'cardio'.

Things bigger than a car.Bus: A city bus is usually about 12 meters long, roughly three times the length of a typical car, so it clearly wins.
Things bigger than a car.Blue whale: The blue whale is the largest animal ever known; it can reach about 30 meters and weigh as much as around 150 tonnes.
Things bigger than a car.House: A house is much bigger than a car, and the average one has about as much floor space as a dozen cars parked together.
Things bigger than a car.Airplane: A jumbo jet is around 70 meters long, with wings bigger than a house, so it is far bigger than any car.
Things bigger than a car.Cruise ship: The largest cruise ships are over 360 meters long, taller than many skyscrapers if stood on end.
Things bigger than a car.Barn: A barn has to be big enough to store a farm's hay, machinery, and animals, so it dwarfs any car.
Things bigger than a car.School bus: A school bus is usually around 10 meters long, and the yellow color was chosen in 1939 because it is easiest to spot.
Things bigger than a car.Lighthouse: Lighthouses commonly stand from 20 to over 100 meters tall, and the tallest, in Saudi Arabia, tops 130 meters.
Things bigger than a car.Train: A freight train can stretch over a kilometer and weigh thousands of tonnes, far more than any car.
Things bigger than a car.Hot air balloon: A hot air balloon can stand about 20 meters tall and hold over 2,000 cubic meters of air, far bigger than a car.
Things bigger than a car.Ferris wheel: The first Ferris wheel, built for the 1893 Chicago fair, was about 80 meters tall and carried over 2,000 passengers.
Things bigger than a car.T. rex: Tyrannosaurus rex was about 12 meters long, and it likely had a bite many times stronger than a lion's.
Things bigger than a car.Bicycle: A bicycle is smaller than a car, but it can carry a person very efficiently, since it is the most energy-efficient transport known.
Things bigger than a car.Cat: A cat is far smaller than a car, but it can jump about five times its own height from a standstill.
Things bigger than a car.Toaster: A toaster is a small kitchen appliance, far smaller than a car, and the first electric one was made in 1909.
Things bigger than a car.Skateboard: A skateboard is under a meter long, much smaller than a car, and the first ones were made around 1950 from wooden boxes and roller skates.
Things bigger than a car.Dog: A dog is smaller than a car, but even the biggest breed, the Great Dane, is under a meter tall at the shoulder.
Things bigger than a car.Piano: A concert grand piano is long and heavy, but it is still only around 3 meters, so a car is bigger.
Things bigger than a car.Fridge: A fridge is much smaller than a car, but it uses the same cooling principle as air conditioners.
Things bigger than a car.Motorcycle: A motorcycle is shorter and lighter than a car, with a typical one being about 2 meters long.
Things bigger than a car.Sofa: A sofa is usually two meters long, so it fits inside a car with the seats down, just about.
Things bigger than a car.Goat: A goat is far smaller than a car, but goats are nimble climbers that can scale near-vertical cliffs.
Things bigger than a car.Lawnmower: A push lawnmower is a small machine, and the first one was patented in 1830 by an English engineer.
Things bigger than a car.Armchair: An armchair is smaller than a car, and it can usually fit in the trunk or back seat of one without trouble.

Things with stripes.Zebra: No two zebras share the same stripe pattern, and the stripes may deter biting flies, which dislike landing on them.
Things with stripes.Tiger: A tiger's stripes are on its skin as well as its fur, and no two tigers have the same pattern.
Things with stripes.Bee: Bees' stripes are a warning: bright yellow-and-black tells predators that these insects can sting.
Things with stripes.Candy cane: Candy canes are traditionally red and white, and the hooked shape is often said to come from a choirmaster handing them out.
Things with stripes.Barber pole: The red and white pole stems from barber-surgeons, who also treated wounds; red stood for blood and white for bandages.
Things with stripes.Referee shirt: Referee stripes began as a way to make officials easy to spot among players; the black-and-white look became a sport icon.
Things with stripes.Zebra crossing: The zebra crossing got its name in Britain in 1951; the stripes are there to show the path to drivers.
Things with stripes.Skunk: A skunk's bold white stripes warn predators about the spray, which can reach about three metres and carry far on the wind.
Things with stripes.Chipmunk: Chipmunks have bold stripes running down their backs and faces and stuff food into pouches that can hold a whole load.
Things with stripes.Clownfish: Clownfish are orange with white stripes, and they live safely among anemone tentacles that sting other fish; they start life as males.
Things with stripes.Watermelon: Watermelons often have stripes on the rind, and the fruit is more than 90 percent water; some are yellow or even seedless.
Things with stripes.Tabby cat: A tabby cat has stripes, and the 'M' marking on the forehead is a classic tabby trait; tabby is a pattern, not a breed.
Things with stripes.Leopard: A trap: leopards have rosettes, not stripes; their spots help them blend into dappled forest light.
Things with stripes.Dalmatian: Dalmatians are born white and are spotted, not striped; the spots show up within weeks.
Things with stripes.Ladybug: Ladybugs are spotted, not striped; their spots warn predators that they are bitter and unpleasant.
Things with stripes.Cheetah: Cheetahs have solid spots rather than stripes, but black tear lines run from their eyes to their mouth.
Things with stripes.Giraffe: Giraffes have patches, not stripes; the okapi, a close relative, does have zebra-like stripes on its legs.
Things with stripes.Polar bear: Polar bears are plain-looking with no stripes; their skin under the fur is black.
Things with stripes.Flamingo: Flamingos are solid pink, not striped; they sleep standing on one leg, which saves body heat.
Things with stripes.Strawberry: Strawberries have seeds on the outside, not stripes; they're not true berries, but the seeds are tiny fruits.
Things with stripes.Lemon: Lemons are plain yellow, with no stripes, though there is a pink variegated lemon whose peel has green stripes.
Things with stripes.Swan: Swans are plain white or black, with no stripes; they often mate for life and pair bond over many years.
Things with stripes.Panda: Pandas have black patches, not stripes, and spend up to 14 hours a day eating bamboo.
Things with stripes.Crow: Crows are solid black, with no stripes, and they're among the cleverest birds, making and using tools.

Things often stuck in trees.Kite: Kites get snared by treetops all the time, and tangled string is the reason this is such a classic problem.
Things often stuck in trees.Cat: Firefighters in many countries say that they rarely rescue cats from trees, since cats can usually climb down on their own, backwards.
Things often stuck in trees.Frisbee: The Frisbee was named for the Frisbie Baking Company's pie tins, which students flung around in the 1940s.
Things often stuck in trees.Balloon: Helium balloons slip into the sky and drift into branches, and they can float for miles before landing.
Things often stuck in trees.Shuttlecock: A badminton shuttlecock has 16 feathers, traditionally from the left wing of a goose, and its light weight lets the wind steer it into branches.
Things often stuck in trees.Paper airplane: Paper airplanes can glide quite far, and a record flight went over 200 feet, so a tree can easily catch one.
Things often stuck in trees.Plastic bag: A plastic bag drifts on the wind and snags on twigs, where it can hang for years.
Things often stuck in trees.Drone: Drones often hit trees when flown too close, and many models now have obstacle-sensing cameras.
Things often stuck in trees.Model rocket: Model rockets use a parachute for recovery, and wind can drift them right into a tall tree.
Things often stuck in trees.Toilet paper: Toilet paper thrown over branches is the classic prank known as 'teepeeing', in which a tree looks wrapped in streamers.
Things often stuck in trees.Car: A car in a tree is rare, but cars have been blown off cliffs; no ordinary event puts one up in branches.
Things often stuck in trees.Bus: A bus is far too heavy to be stuck in a tree, and a typical bus weighs over ten tons.
Things often stuck in trees.Piano: A piano weighs hundreds of pounds, so it won't end up in a tree on its own.
Things often stuck in trees.Swimming pool: A swimming pool is dug in the ground and holds thousands of gallons, so it can't get stuck.
Things often stuck in trees.Elephant: An elephant is the largest land animal and weighs several tons, so no tree could hold one.
Things often stuck in trees.Refrigerator: A refrigerator weighs about as much as a person or two and doesn't get stuck by accident.
Things often stuck in trees.Fire hydrant: Fire hydrants are bolted to the ground, which makes them unlikely to end up in a tree.
Things often stuck in trees.Mailbox: A mailbox is fixed on a post, so it doesn't move on its own to a tree.
Things often stuck in trees.Lawnmower: A lawnmower is heavy, ground-bound machinery, and is not something that gets stuck in a tree.
Things often stuck in trees.Bathtub: A bathtub of cast iron can weigh hundreds of pounds, so it won't blow into a tree.
Things often stuck in trees.Train: A train runs on rails, and a locomotive weighs well over a hundred tons.
Things often stuck in trees.Snowman: A snowman melts in spring, and wouldn't be flung into a tree.
Things often stuck in trees.Sofa: A sofa is heavy, and wind won't carry one into a tree, though it's a standard flood-debris item.
Things often stuck in trees.Hippo: A hippo can weigh several tons, so no tree is hoisting one.

Jobs that wear a uniform.Police officer: Uniforms make officers easy to spot in emergencies. Britain's first modern force, founded in 1829, wore blue coats so they'd not be mistaken for soldiers.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Firefighter: Their heavy turnout gear can weigh around 30 pounds with equipment. It's designed to resist intense heat for long enough to escape.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Pilot: Airline pilots' uniforms with striped epaulettes follow naval tradition, a style adopted when early air travel borrowed from ships.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Nurse: Florence Nightingale's work made nursing a trained profession. Colored scrubs today often show hospital department or rank.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Soldier: Camouflage uniforms are a modern invention, as armies once wore bright colors. The shift came as rifles made visibility deadly.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Mail carrier: US carriers follow an unofficial motto about rain and snow, which is inscribed on New York's main post office.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Flight attendant: They're onboard mainly for safety, and their training covers evacuation, firefighting and first aid, well beyond serving drinks.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Security guard: Their uniforms are meant to signal authority. The look often mimics police dress, though their legal powers are generally far narrower.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Paramedic: Many wear a 'Star of Life', a blue six-armed symbol with the Rod of Asclepius at its center, adopted in the US in 1970.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Chef: The tall white toque is said to have up to 100 pleats, supposedly one for each way to cook an egg. Whites hide no stains by design.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Park ranger: US rangers wear a flat-brimmed hat called a campaign hat, which has been part of the National Park Service look since early days.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Referee: Black and white stripes became standard so officials stand out. FIFA referees now often wear other colors to avoid clashing with teams.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Novelist: Writers choose their own clothes. Plenty of authors, from Hemingway to Murakami, have famously kept strict daily routines but no dress code.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Painter: Some artists wear smocks, but there's no uniform. The beret cliché largely came from 19th-century Paris.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Freelancer: They work for themselves, so dress is whatever suits them. Surveys regularly show many freelancers work in casual clothes.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Poet: Poets have no set dress, though Romantics like Byron made loose open collars fashionable.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Blogger: No official uniform exists. The word 'blog' began as 'weblog' in the late 1990s before being shortened.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Philosopher: Ancient Greek thinkers sometimes wore plain cloaks as a statement. Diogenes famously lived in a large jar and owned little.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Influencer: Their 'uniform' is personal style. They emerged with social media, and brand deals now shape what they wear.
Jobs that wear a uniform.Composer: Composers dress as they please. Beethoven's famously untidy look matched his chaotic rooms.
